century.html.head: 6f9b709e72cc618bd2a4b13338a31a50ed76233f1d166c85caa75c4cd863bb7a
text: A corporate AI platform for controlled work.
Century is a product surface between AI consumers and the models, data and infrastructure underneath: chat, agents, workflows, APIs, protected data access and operational controls.
Models are only one part of the operating system.
Enterprise AI also needs controlled access to company data, a place for users and systems to work with it, a deployment boundary, and enough logs and policy to review what happened.
Chat, constructors and APIs give teams a shared product surface for AI work.
Documents, databases and internal services can be connected within defined access boundaries.
Roles, policies, logs and traces make AI activity visible for operation and review.
Capabilities currently described by the product source.
Internal chat and AI assistants for employees, customers and operational work.
Workflow and automation modes for repeatable steps, escalation and human participation.
Document search with source links plus natural-language access to structured business data.
Connections to internal databases and corporate services through APIs, queues and protected connectors.
Capability wording is based on the current Century product site and may change as the product evolves.
A protected contour around models, data and work.

The product site describes isolated instances on customer servers, on-premise, VPC and private-cloud options. It also describes local processing, policy checks before data access, and integration through protected connectors.
Local processing inside the controlled contour
AI consumers → Century entry point → security, data and compliance guarantees → models, data and infrastructure → protected deployment contour.
The system is reviewable because activity leaves a trace.
Role-based access and policy controls are part of the described product boundary.
Requests, models, tokens and costs can be logged for operational review and audit work.
The product source describes protections against data leakage and prompt injection; implementation depends on the deployment context.
Product context, not an invented personal title.

Century is the product anchor for the governed-private-AI positioning on this site. Public product material describes capabilities and recognition; it does not establish Vadim's exact Century title or personal ownership, so this page does not assign one.
Century received third place in the AI Product Leader category at IT-Akademgrad 2025. This is product recognition, not a personal award.
No live adoption count, client case, roadmap promise, personal title or deployment outcome is added without a confirmed source.

text: Private AI systems for regulated organisations.
A decision-led way to move from use-case selection to controlled production: define the boundary, make ownership explicit, and design the system that people can review and operate.
The decisions an enterprise AI initiative has to survive.
Choose a workflow where data, ownership, review and value can be made explicit.
Decide how models, retrieval, integrations, access and deployment boundaries fit together.
Define evaluation, human review, source grounding, audit and escalation before rollout.
Make product, security, engineering and risk responsibilities visible after the pilot.
From a priority decision to a controlled production boundary.

Map product scope, architecture, access boundaries, evaluation and review.
Use source-grounded scenarios and operational checks to expose risk early.
Set ownership, observability, escalation and deployment controls for the next boundary.
This is a method for making a decision and its constraints explicit; it is not a guarantee of delivery or an implied client case.
Controls belong in the product and operating model.

The relevant questions are practical: who can access which data, how sources are grounded, when a human reviews an output, what is logged, what is observable, and which deployment model is acceptable.

text: When product, architecture and engineering diverge.
A practical diagnostic for founders who need to identify the real constraint, make ownership explicit and choose a credible next operating plan.
You may need a diagnostic when…
Product commitments depend on technical decisions nobody has made explicit.
The team is active, but delivery, ownership and review remain unclear.
Pilot work cannot become a product
AI scope is larger than the evidence, workflow or operating model can support.
Engineering risks, integration questions or unclear ownership make the next promise unsafe.
Architecture, product and team trade-offs are revisited without a shared decision map.
There is no agreed sequence for what to fix, test, defer or own next.
Start with the decision, then inspect the system around it.
Clarify the product decision and operating constraint
Review product scope, architecture, information and ownership
Prioritise risks by consequence and reversibility
Agree the next cadence, decision owners and checks
Concrete outputs for the next operating decision.

Where product scope, system design and engineering reality have separated.

investors.html.head: 9c59306777d251eb1ec10481cf1122cb4c176896da33c273b568b3957469a034
text: A practical assessment of whether an AI product, its data, architecture, team and deployment claims can survive real operating conditions.
Does the technical story hold together?

The assessment asks whether the product solves a real workflow, whether the data position is defensible, whether the architecture and team can support the claims, and what remains unproven before a decision.
What exists beyond the demo, and which workflow is actually supported?
Are data rights, feedback loops, model choices and RAG quality clear?
Can integrations, security, governance and observability survive deployment?
Can the team make trade-offs, expose technical debt and ship the next boundary?
What changes when the product enters a customer's real environment?
What is measured, what is expensive, and what can the team see in operation?
Which product, data, security or delivery statements still need evidence?
Examples here are assessment questions. They are not claims about a completed review, a portfolio or a transaction.
Architecture and repository review when permitted
Risk register with red flags and open questions
Written technical memo and decision briefing
A written view of what is known, open and risky.
What was looked at, what was supplied, and which questions remain open.
Architecture, data, deployment, observability, team execution and hidden technical debt.
Red flags, open questions, limitations and the next technical checks to run.

This work is a technical assessment of product, data, architecture, deployment and team claims. It is not legal, financial, accounting or regulated investment advice, and it does not allocate capital, recommend a transaction or guarantee an outcome.
